title: Hereditary Genius: An Inquiry into Its Laws and Consequences
authors: Francis Galton
key_findings: (via Wozniak introduction, read) used eminence/reputation as a proxy for ability; found eminence far more common among relatives of eminent men, declining with kinship distance; first statistical treatment of genius
practical_applications: History only: origin of the quantitative / individual-differences study of exceptional achievement
limitations: Eminence confounds ability with opportunity, class and family environment; tied to the eugenics programme; Wozniak intro does not cover critiques; book itself not read

title: The Art of Thought
authors: Graham Wallas
key_findings: Ch. 4 (read): names four stages Preparation, Incubation, Illumination (with its accompaniments) and Verification, built from Helmholtz and Poincare self-reports; adds Intimation as the fringe-conscious feeling that precedes the flash
Quotes Poincare: unconscious work only gives points of departure; the working-out must be done consciously in Verification
practical_applications: Use stages as a scheduling heuristic (prepare hard, step away, verify consciously), not as a fixed law
limitations: Built on anecdotes of eminent men, not experiments; only chapter 4 read

title: Creativity
authors: Guilford, J. P.
key_findings: APA presidential address (American Psychologist 5(9):444-454) credited with starting psychological creativity research; Guilford's later Structure-of-Intellect model separates divergent from convergent production.
practical_applications: Separate a 'generate many' phase from a 'pick one' phase.
limitations: Known through secondary sources only; full text not read.
Reused record from an earlier batch (key kept); not re-read in this session.

title: Applied Imagination: Principles and Procedures of Creative Thinking
authors: Alex F. Osborn
key_findings: (via secondary summaries) brainstorming rests on two principles, defer judgment and reach for quantity; four rules: no criticism, quantity, welcome wild ideas, combine and improve
practical_applications: Keep the two principles (defer judgment, quantity) but drop the group-talk format: generate alone first
limitations: Book not read; the claim that groups produce more ideas was later refuted by nominal-group studies

title: The Creativity Crisis: The Decrease in Creative Thinking Scores on the Torrance Tests of Creative Thinking
authors: Kyung Hee Kim
key_findings: TTCT developed 1966, renormed 1974-2008; 272,599 K-12 students and adults in six normative samples
Scores static or falling from 6th grade; since 1990 scores fell while IQ rose; largest drop K-3
practical_applications: Background for why TTCT matters; do not use as proof of any cause
limitations: Normative samples are not the same cohorts; causes not tested

title: Torrance Tests of Creative Thinking as Predictors of Personal and Public Achievement: A Fifty-Year Follow-Up
authors: Mark A. Runco, Garnet Millar, Selcuk Acar, Bonnie Cramond
key_findings: TTCT given late 1950s; 50 years later scores moderately correlated with personal but not public achievement
Intelligence x creativity interaction related to public achievement; "love of work", tolerance of mistakes, "minority of one" related to public achievement
practical_applications: Divergent-thinking scores are a weak, partial predictor; persistence and tolerance of mistakes matter for public output
limitations: Single longitudinal cohort; attrition; self-reported achievement

title: The social psychology of creativity: A componential conceptualization
authors: Teresa M. Amabile
key_findings: Componential framework: domain-relevant skills, creativity-relevant skills and task motivation as necessary components; social environment affects stages of the process
practical_applications: Diagnose a stuck project by component: missing domain skill, missing technique, or missing motivation
limitations: A framework, not a tested causal model; later revised (Amabile & Pratt 2016, not read)

title: Social psychology of creativity: A consensual assessment technique
authors: Teresa M. Amabile
key_findings: (via Cseh & Jeffries) independent expert judges rating relative to the sample reach acceptable agreement; collage study: psychologists .73, art teachers .88
practical_applications: Use several independent judges who rate without discussion, items in different random orders
limitations: Not read directly
Existence and DOI confirmed via Crossref this session; content via Cseh & Jeffries 2019 and Kaufman et al. 2009 abstracts.

title: Society, Culture, and Person: A Systems View of Creativity (in Sternberg ed., The Nature of Creativity; reprinted 2014 in The Systems Model of Creativity)
authors: Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi
key_findings: (via search summaries) creativity arises from the interaction of person, domain (symbolic rules) and field (gatekeepers who select what enters the domain)
practical_applications: Treat audience, client, platform and peers as the field that decides what counts as creative
limitations: Chapter not read; theoretical, not experimentally tested

title: Creativity and artificial intelligence
authors: Margaret A. Boden
key_findings: Three types: combinational (improbable combinations of familiar ideas), exploratory (search within a conceptual space), transformational (changing dimensions of the space so previously impossible ideas become possible)
P-creativity (new to the person/system) vs H-creativity (new to history); P is the more fundamental notion
AI handles exploratory best; the hardest part is automating evaluation, not generation
practical_applications: Label each direction as combinational / exploratory / transformational to check the set is really different; keep evaluation with humans
limitations: Read via a mirror HTML copy (publisher page returned 403); 1998 view predates LLMs

title: Creativity and Discovery as Blind Variation: Campbell's (1960) BVSR Model after the Half-Century Mark
authors: Dean Keith Simonton
key_findings: Defends and extends Campbell 1960 BVSR; defines blind variation by superfluity and backtracking and by processes such as associative richness, defocused attention, tinkering and heuristic search
practical_applications: Generate more variants than you need and expect to throw most away; selection is a separate step
limitations: Contested: see Gabora 2011; "blindness" is hard to operationalise

title: An Analysis of the Blind Variation and Selective Retention Theory of Creativity
authors: Liane Gabora
key_findings: Using Picasso Guernica sketches: lack of similarity between successive sketches is not evidence of selection; ideas are modified as they are thought through, so a selectionist frame does not fit; biases from expertise and remote association make variation non-blind
practical_applications: Iteration is honing of one idea, not only picking among random variants: keep both modes
limitations: Theoretical critique; Simonton replied (sightedness)

title: Beyond Big and Little: The Four C Model of Creativity
authors: James C. Kaufman, Ronald A. Beghetto
key_findings: Adds mini-c (creativity in learning) and Pro-c (professional-level) to little-c (everyday) and Big-C (eminent)
practical_applications: Studio work is Pro-c: judged by a professional field and audience, not by eminence
limitations: Conceptual model

title: The Bias Against Creativity: Why People Desire but Reject Creative Ideas
authors: Jennifer S. Mueller, Shimul Melwani, Jack A. Goncalo
key_findings: Creative ideas are defined as both novel and useful
Exp 1 (N=73): uncertainty (lottery) produced an implicit (IAT) bias against creativity relative to practicality; explicit attitudes unchanged
Exp 2 (N=140): low tolerance for uncertainty raised implicit bias and lowered creativity ratings of a pre-tested creative idea (5.06 vs 5.76 on 7-pt); partial mediation
practical_applications: When the client/user is anxious or rushed, novel options are under-rated: reduce uncertainty (show a mock-up, a reference, a test plan) before presenting the bold option
limitations: Two small student samples; IAT measure validity debated; no large replication found in this search

title: The associative basis of the creative process
authors: Mednick, S. A.
key_findings: Creativity = combining associative elements into new useful combinations; the more remote the elements, the more creative; proposed flatter associative hierarchies in creative people (basis of the Remote Associates Test).
Benedek & Neubauer (2013, PMC3924568) found hierarchies did not differ, but creative people showed higher associative fluency and more uncommon responses.
practical_applications: Deliberately pair distant domains (eyewear x temple fair, glasses x weather) to push past first associations.
limitations: No abstract; content via secondary sources; core hierarchy hypothesis only partly supported.
DOI confirmed via Crossref this session; content from earlier batch.

title: Structure-mapping: A theoretical framework for analogy
authors: Dedre Gentner
key_findings: Analogy maps relations between objects, not object attributes, from base to target
Which relations map is governed by systematicity (connected higher-order relations)
practical_applications: A good analogy for a story or ad shares a relational structure (cause, conflict, change), not surface looks
limitations: Theory of interpretation, not of how analogies are found

title: Conceptual Integration Networks
authors: Fauconnier, G.; Turner, M.
key_findings: Blending is a general cognitive operation: two input spaces, a generic space and a blended space with emergent structure; network types simplex, mirror, single-scope, double-scope. Cognitive Science 22(2):133-187.
practical_applications: Visual metaphors (lens = window, frame = character) as deliberate blends; check the blend's emergent meaning reads clearly.
limitations: Secondary summaries only; theory, little predictive experimental test.
Reused record from an earlier batch (key kept); not re-read in this session.

title: Analogical problem solving
authors: Gick, M. L.; Holyoak, K. J.
key_findings: People who read a military story often transferred its solution to Duncker's radiation problem only when hinted; without a hint analogous solutions dropped markedly; Gick & Holyoak 1983: two analogues improve transfer (schema induction).
practical_applications: Analogies do not arrive by themselves: explicitly ask 'what else works like this?' and give 2+ source examples from different domains.
limitations: Abstract and secondary summaries; exact transfer rates not captured.
Reused record from an earlier batch (key kept); not re-read in this session.

title: Does Incubation Enhance Problem Solving? A Meta-Analytic Review
authors: Sio, U. N.; Ormerod, T. C.
key_findings: 117 studies, 3,606 participants; weighted mean incubation effect 0.29 (95% CI 0.21-0.39); no publication bias detected by regression of effect on sample size
Divergent-thinking (creative) tasks benefit more than linguistic or visual insight tasks
Longer preparation periods give larger effects; high-demand incubation tasks give smaller effects; low-demand tasks beat rest for linguistic problems
practical_applications: Work the brief hard first, then switch to a low-demand task and come back before final selection.
limitations: Abstract and secondary summaries; lab puzzles.
Full text read this session (author PDF).

title: Inspired by Distraction: Mind Wandering Facilitates Creative Incubation
authors: Benjamin Baird, Jonathan Smallwood, Michael D. Mrazek, Julia W. Y. Kam, Michael S. Franklin, Jonathan W. Schooler
key_findings: An undemanding task during incubation improved Unusual Uses performance on previously seen problems, versus demanding task, rest or no break; associated with more mind wandering, not more explicit thought about the task
practical_applications: Historical claim behind "take a walk"; see failed replications
limitations: Conceptual replications failed (Murray et al. 2024)

title: What are the benefits of mind wandering to creativity?
authors: Samuel Murray, Nathan Liang, Nicholaus Brosowsky, Paul Seli
key_findings: Conceptual replication of Baird et al. 2012 across two studies (N=443): no evidence that mind wandering during incubation helps divergent thinking
Argue task-unrelated thought is unlikely to be causally related to creativity
practical_applications: Keep the break (incubation has meta-analytic support) but do not claim mind wandering is the mechanism
limitations: Conceptual not direct replication; DT tasks only

title: The Cognitive Neuroscience of Insight
authors: John Kounios, Mark Beeman
key_findings: Insight = sudden reinterpretation producing a nonobvious, nondominant interpretation (solution, joke, metaphor, ambiguous percept)
Linked to right-hemisphere coarse semantic coding and internally focused attention; resting-state differences between insightful and analytic solvers
practical_applications: A punchline or story twist works as engineered insight: set up the dominant reading, then allow the non-dominant one
limitations: Neuroimaging of insight has been critiqued (Weisberg 2013, title seen only); hemisphere claims should not be overstated

title: Insight solutions are correct more often than analytic solutions
authors: Carola Salvi, Emanuela Bricolo, John Kounios, Edward Bowden, Mark Beeman
key_findings: In four experiments self-judged insight solutions were more accurate than analytic ones; analytic responses had more errors of commission
practical_applications: An "aha" on a small puzzle is informative, but it does not validate a whole campaign idea: still test with the audience
limitations: Lab puzzles; does not transfer to judging creative quality

title: Design fixation
authors: Jansson, D. G.; Smith, S. M.
key_findings: Showing an example solution made designers (incl. professionals) repeat its features, even flawed ones; instructions to avoid the features did not reduce fixation.
Mixed later evidence: Purcell et al. 1993 replications largely unsuccessful, effects tied to familiarity; Chrysikou & Weisberg found defixation instructions helped.
practical_applications: Reference images and AI drafts anchor us; generate own directions before looking at references or AI output.
limitations: Known via secondary papers (Design Studies); replication mixed - medium confidence.

Existence/DOI 10.1016/0142-694x(91)90003-f confirmed via Crossref this session; summaries via design-fixation literature search (Purcell & Gero 1996: fixation in mechanical-engineering but not industrial-design students).

title: Constraining effects of examples in a creative generation task
authors: Steven M. Smith, Thomas B. Ward, Jay S. Schumacher
key_findings: (via search summaries of the paper) in three experiments, people who saw examples produced designs containing more example features; instructions to make designs unlike the examples did not reduce conformity; a 23-minute interpolated task reduced it
practical_applications: Do the first idea round before opening references or AI images; if you must see examples, wait before generating
limitations: Not read directly; lab drawing task with students

title: Inspiration and fixation: Questions, methods, findings, and challenges
authors: Luis A. Vasconcelos, Nathan Crilly
key_findings: Review of 25 experimental studies: 14 manipulated variables; great variety in methods and results; calls for harmonised methods
practical_applications: Treat "examples cause fixation" as a real risk with uncertain size, not a law
limitations: Narrative review, not meta-analysis

title: Creativity and Innovation Under Constraints: A Cross-Disciplinary Integrative Review
authors: Acar, O. A.; Tarakci, M.; van Knippenberg, D.
key_findings: Constraint research across management fields is fragmented with conflicting findings; builds a taxonomy of constraints and mediating mechanisms (motivation, cognition, social context).
practical_applications: Constraints are not automatically good or bad; pick constraints that force search away from defaults (e.g., 'no coffee shop, no sunset').
limitations: Abstract only; taxonomy categories not verified; the common 'inverted-U' summary was not confirmed this session.
Reused record from an earlier batch (key kept); not re-read in this session.

title: The Green Eggs and Ham hypothesis: How constraints facilitate creativity
authors: Catrinel Haught-Tromp
key_findings: (via search summaries) two experiments: 2-line rhymes that had to include given nouns were rated more creative than unconstrained ones; constraints cut choices to a manageable subset
practical_applications: Give each direction one precise constraint (a required object/word) rather than "anything goes"
limitations: Not read directly; student samples, one task type

title: The role of deliberate practice in the acquisition of expert performance
authors: K. Anders Ericsson; Ralf Th. Krampe; Clemens Tesch-Roemer
key_findings: Expert performance explained as the result of prolonged deliberate practice: effortful activities designed to improve performance
Individual differences even among elites closely related to assessed amounts of deliberate practice
practical_applications: Design practice that targets a weakness with feedback, not just more output
limitations: Retrospective practice estimates; core finding not replicated by Macnamara & Maitra 2019
Abstract read this session via OpenAlex.

title: Deliberate Practice and Performance in Music, Games, Sports, Education, and Professions: A Meta-Analysis
authors: Brooke N. Macnamara; David Z. Hambrick; Frederick L. Oswald
key_findings: Deliberate practice explained 26% of performance variance in games, 21% music, 18% sports, 4% education, <1% professions
Deliberate practice is important but not as important as argued
practical_applications: Do not promise that logging lessons alone makes a studio excellent; measure outcomes
limitations: Definition of deliberate practice disputed by Ericsson & Harwell 2019
Abstract read this session via Crossref.

title: The role of deliberate practice in expert performance: revisiting Ericsson, Krampe & Tesch-Romer (1993)
authors: Brooke N. Macnamara, Megha Maitra
key_findings: Double-blind replication with violinists did not replicate the core finding that accumulated deliberate practice corresponded to each skill level
practical_applications: Do not promise "10,000 hours" or "10 years" to anyone
limitations: Single domain, small sample of violinists

title: Cognitive Processes in Creativity (in Glover, Ronning & Reynolds eds., Handbook of Creativity)
authors: John R. Hayes
key_findings: (via secondary summaries) of 76 classical composers almost all needed at least ten years of intensive study before a first masterwork; three exceptions at years 8-9
practical_applications: Long apprenticeship in a domain is the norm for masterworks
limitations: Chapter not read; eminence sample; date given as 1989 or 1990 in different sources

title: Creative Development as Acquired Expertise: Theoretical Issues and an Empirical Test
authors: Dean Keith Simonton
key_findings: (via secondary summaries) in classical composers the expertise period is an average with large variance; the most eminent took less time than average
practical_applications: The 10-year rule is an average, not a rule
limitations: Not read directly; historiometric sample of famous composers

title: Working Memory Benefits Creative Insight, Musical Improvisation, and Original Ideation Through Maintained Task-Focused Attention
authors: Carsten K. W. De Dreu, Bernard A. Nijstad, Matthijs Baas, Inge Wolsink, Marieke Roskes
key_findings: Under cognitive load people did worse on a creative insight task
Working-memory capacity predicted creativity via persistence (focused, systematic combining), including in cellists' improvisations
practical_applications: Do not ideate while juggling render queues and chats; protect a focused block for generation
limitations: Four studies, moderate samples; dual-pathway model

title: Intelligence, creativity, and cognitive control: The common and differential involvement of executive functions in intelligence and creativity
authors: Mathias Benedek, Emanuel Jauk, Markus Sommer, Martin Arendasy, Aljoscha C. Neubauer
key_findings: Latent-variable study: divergent thinking predicted by updating and inhibition, not shifting; updating (and openness) explains shared variance between intelligence and creativity
practical_applications: Originality needs suppression of the obvious answer (inhibition): write down and ban the default first
limitations: Cross-sectional; DT tasks as the creativity measure

title: Robust prediction of individual creative ability from brain functional connectivity
authors: Roger E. Beaty, Yoed N. Kenett, Alexander P. Christensen, Monica D. Rosenberg, Mathias Benedek, et al.
key_findings: A network spanning default, salience and executive systems predicted originality of ideas across four independent datasets
practical_applications: Supports the view that creative ideation combines spontaneous generation with controlled evaluation
limitations: Correlational; DT task as criterion; not a training recipe

title: A review of EEG, ERP, and neuroimaging studies of creativity and insight
authors: Arne Dietrich, Riam Kanso
key_findings: 72 experiments in 63 articles; divergent-thinking and artistic-creativity neural findings inconsistent; insight findings more consistent (anterior cingulate, prefrontal); creativity not localised in one region
practical_applications: Reject "right-brain creative" claims in copy and training
limitations: Pre-2010 literature; qualitative synthesis

title: How the Group Affects the Mind: A Cognitive Model of Idea Generation in Groups
authors: Bernard A. Nijstad, Wolfgang Stroebe
key_findings: SIAM model: idea generation = repeated search of associative memory (knowledge activation, then idea production); turn-taking (production blocking) interferes with both stages; others' ideas can aid activation; cognitive failures drive persistence and satisfaction
practical_applications: Read others' ideas only after your own round, as stimulation for a second round
limitations: Model; tested mostly in lab groups

title: Productivity Loss in Brainstorming Groups: Toward the Solution of a Riddle
authors: Diehl, M.; Stroebe, W.
key_findings: Four experiments: production blocking (waiting to speak) accounted for most of the productivity loss of interactive vs nominal groups; free riding and evaluation apprehension were minor.
practical_applications: Generate alone first, then pool (nominal group / brainwriting).
limitations: Abstract/secondary only; lab tasks, students.
Reused record from an earlier batch (key kept); not re-read in this session.

title: Productivity Loss in Brainstorming Groups: A Meta-Analytic Integration
authors: Mullen, B.; Johnson, C.; Salas, E.
key_findings: Interactive brainstorming groups produce fewer and lower-quality ideas than nominal groups; losses grow with group size, experimenter presence and spoken (vs written) ideas.
practical_applications: Classic 'everyone shout ideas' brainstorming is the weakest format; write ideas individually.
limitations: Abstract only; Diehl & Stroebe disputed some mechanism conclusions.
Reused record from an earlier batch (key kept); not re-read in this session.

title: Idea Generation and the Quality of the Best Idea
authors: Girotra, K.; Terwiesch, C.; Ulrich, K. T.
key_findings: Hybrid structure (work alone, then pool and evaluate as a team) beat team-only on number of ideas, quality, and ability to discern the best idea; building on others' ideas did not yield more or better ideas.
Best-idea quality depends on mean quality, number, variance, and selection ability.
practical_applications: We need the best idea, not the average: maximise variance in generation, then select carefully with criteria.
limitations: Abstract only; lab product-idea task.
Reused record from an earlier batch (key kept); not re-read in this session.

title: Balancing on the Creative Highwire: Forecasting the Success of Novel Ideas in Organizations
authors: Justin M. Berg
key_findings: 339 circus professionals forecast audience success of new acts, checked against 13,248 audience members
Creators forecast peers' novel ideas more accurately than managers, but overestimated their own
Managers undervalued novel acts; best judges were peers who generate ideas but did not make the one judged; lab study: creator mindset improved ranking of novel ideas
practical_applications: Use peer creators (another agent/person who also makes work) as critics; never the author alone
limitations: Circus domain; read via Stanford GSB summary, not the ASQ paper
Abstract read this session via Crossref.

title: Idea evaluation: Error in evaluating highly original ideas
authors: Brian F. Licuanan, Lesley R. Dailey, Michael D. Mumford
key_findings: 181 undergraduates evaluating marketing campaigns tended to underestimate the originality of highly novel ideas; active analysis of product originality and of team process reduced the error
practical_applications: Score originality explicitly as its own criterion instead of an overall gut rating
limitations: Student raters; one task

title: Errors in Idea Evaluation: Preference for the Unoriginal?
authors: Cassie S. Blair, Michael D. Mumford
key_findings: Evaluators preferred ideas that were easy to understand, gave short-term benefits to many and fit social norms, and disregarded risky, time-consuming, original ideas; original/risky ideas were preferred more when criteria were less stringent and time pressure high
practical_applications: Expect clients to pick the safest option; present the bold one with its risk handled
limitations: Student samples, foundation-funding scenario

title: Expertise, Domains, and the Consensual Assessment Technique
authors: James C. Kaufman, John Baer, Jason C. Cole
key_findings: Expert vs novice ratings of short fiction correlated only .71; experts far more consistent; novice inter-rater reliability potentially problematic; (via summary) CAT reliability typically .80-.90 and rises with number of judges
practical_applications: Use several independent raters, ideally with domain experience; do not trust one rater
limitations: One domain (fiction)

title: A scattered CAT: A critical evaluation of the Consensual Assessment Technique for creativity research
authors: Genevieve M. Cseh, Karl K. Jeffries
key_findings: CAT guidelines: judges with domain experience, rate independently without training or discussion, rate relative to the sample, see items in different random orders, rate other dimensions (technical, aesthetic) separately
Expert vs novice agreement is equivocal and domain-dependent; adding judges (>10) can inflate alpha; <5 judges risks both error types
Reporting of CAT procedures is inconsistent; calls for harmonised protocol
practical_applications: Studio panel: 3-5 independent raters (human + different AI models) rating relatively, before any discussion
limitations: Review of research use, not of studio practice
Abstract read this session via OpenAlex.

title: Assessing creativity with divergent thinking tasks: Exploring the reliability and validity of new subjective scoring methods
authors: Paul J. Silvia, Beate P. Winterstein, John T. Willse, Christopher M. Barona, Joshua T. Cram, et al.
key_findings: Top-2 scoring: participants circle their two most creative responses, raters score 1-5; 2-3 raters give dependable scores; n=226; over half of DT variance explained by personality
practical_applications: Let the creator nominate their best 2 of N before others judge; rate on a 1-5 scale with 2-3 raters
limitations: Student sample; lab DT tasks

title: "Most advanced, yet acceptable": Typicality and novelty as joint predictors of aesthetic preference in industrial design
authors: Paul Hekkert, Dirk Snelders, Piet C. W. van Wieringen
key_findings: Typicality and novelty jointly and equally predict preference for products but suppress each other; people prefer novel designs as long as the novelty does not hurt typicality; expertise did not change this
practical_applications: Audience test for a bold direction: is it still recognisable as its category (a glasses ad, a Mint & Tao story)?
limitations: Product designs; samples from one country

title: Generative AI enhances individual creativity but reduces the collective diversity of novel content
authors: Doshi, A. R.; Hauser, O. P.
key_findings: 293 writers, 600 evaluators; conditions 0, 1 or 5 GPT-4 ideas. Novelty +5.4% (1 idea) and +8.1% (5 ideas); usefulness +3.7% / +9.0%.
Gains largest for less creative writers (novelty up to +10.7%), roughly equalising them with more creative writers.
Stories became more similar to each other (+10.7% / +8.9% of similarity range) and about 5% more similar to the AI ideas - a social dilemma: individuals better off, collective diversity down.
practical_applications: AI ideas raise the floor but pull everyone toward the same stories: use AI for volume/critique, but force divergence (different seeds, constraints, human-first idea) and check against our own past output.
limitations: 8-sentence stories, one LLM, no interaction with the model, UK online sample, opt-in idea use.
Reused record from an earlier batch (key kept); not re-read in this session.

title: Generative AI and Creativity: A Systematic Literature Review and Meta-Analysis
authors: Niklas Holzner, Sebastian Maier, Stefan Feuerriegel
key_findings: 28 studies, 8,214 participants: GenAI alone vs humans g = -0.05 (ns); humans+GenAI vs humans alone g = 0.27; diversity of ideas g = -0.86 (homogenisation)
practical_applications: Use AI to raise individual output but add explicit diversity steps (many directions, human selection, references outside the model)
limitations: Preprint; mostly text/ideation tasks, not images
Abstract read this session (arXiv preprint, not peer reviewed).

title: The Effects of Generative AI on Design Fixation and Divergent Thinking
authors: Samangi Wadinambiarachchi, Ryan M. Kelly, Saumya Pareek, Qiushi Zhou, Eduardo Velloso
key_findings: Between-participants (N=60) visual ideation: AI image generator support led to higher fixation on the initial example, fewer ideas, less variety and lower originality than baseline
Outcome depended on how people wrote prompts and used AI suggestions; (via search snippet) fixation can shift from the exemplar onto the AI outputs
practical_applications: Sketch/write own directions before prompting an image model; use AI after, to execute or to stress-test
limitations: Small N; one task; Midjourney 2023 version

title: Human Creativity in the Age of LLMs: Randomized Experiments on Divergent and Convergent Thinking
authors: Harsh Kumar, Jonathan Vincentius, Ewan Jordan, Ashton Anderson
key_findings: Two pre-registered experiments (1,100 participants): standard LLM or coach-like LLM help boosted performance while assisted but could hurt later unassisted creative performance
practical_applications: Keep regular no-AI ideation rounds so own skill does not decay
limitations: Short online tasks; effects on professionals unknown

title: How AI Ideas Affect the Creativity, Diversity, and Evolution of Human Ideas: Evidence From a Large, Dynamic Experiment
authors: Joshua Ashkinaze, Julia Mendelsohn, Li Qiwei, Ceren Budak, Eric Gilbert
key_findings: 800+ participants, 40+ countries; high exposure to ChatGPT example ideas did not change individual creativity but increased collective idea diversity; disclosure of AI source had no main effect
practical_applications: AI ideas shown as varied stimuli (not as answers to copy) can widen a pool
limitations: Preprint; one task family

title: An empirical investigation of the impact of ChatGPT on creativity
authors: Byung Cheol Lee, Jaeyeon Chung
key_findings: Five experiments: ideas made with ChatGPT (GPT-3.5) rated more creative than with Google or no technology; most effective for incremental, not radically new, ideas; ChatGPT combines remote concepts into a cohesive, articulated form
practical_applications: Use LLMs to polish and articulate incremental ideas; do not rely on them for the radical direction
limitations: Set diversity contested by Meincke et al. 2025 (authors replied, 2025)

title: ChatGPT decreases idea diversity in brainstorming
authors: Lennart Meincke, Gideon Nave, Christian Terwiesch
key_findings: (via Wharton Mack Institute summary) across five experiments ChatGPT-assisted brainstorming produced less diverse idea sets; 37 of 45 comparisons significant; in one task 94% of ChatGPT-assisted ideas shared overlapping concepts and nine participants named their toy "Build-a-Breeze Castle"; one experiment showed no clear drop
practical_applications: Measure set diversity, not just individual idea quality; ask the model for many ideas that differ from each other
limitations: Paper not read; institutional summary only

title: Generative artificial intelligence, human creativity, and art
authors: Eric Zhou, Dokyun Lee
key_findings: 4M+ artworks, ~53,000 artists, ~5,800 AI adopters; difference-in-differences
Productivity up (~50% in adoption month); favourites per view up from ~2% to ~3% by month 6
Average content novelty and average + peak visual novelty declined (convergence to a preferred style); peak content novelty marginally rose
Artists rewarded for exploring new concepts with AI, penalised for using AI to explore new visual styles
practical_applications: The 'AI look' is measurable convergence of visual style: put novelty in the idea and keep a deliberate house style
limitations: Observational; one platform; adoption detected by tags; process not observed
Abstract read this session via Crossref (registry has a full_text record from an earlier batch).

title: Prompting Diverse Ideas: Increasing AI Idea Variance
authors: Meincke, L.; Mollick, E.; Terwiesch, C.
key_findings: GPT-4 with minimal prompting produced less diverse idea pools than groups of humans; personas and creativity-technique prompts helped somewhat; chain-of-thought prompting gave the highest diversity, close to human groups.
Authors suggest using multiple models to add variety.
practical_applications: Ask the model to first list many distinct concepts briefly, then develop each; mix models (Claude/Codex/FLUX) and seeds.
limitations: Working paper (SSRN/arXiv); diversity measured by embeddings, not by audience response; product-idea domain.
Reused record from an earlier batch (key kept); not re-read in this session.

title: Homogenization Effects of Large Language Models on Human Creative Ideation
authors: Anderson, B. R.; Shah, J. H.; Kreminski, M.
key_findings: 36 participants, four TTCT-style divergent tasks: different users produced less semantically distinct ideas with ChatGPT than with a non-AI creativity support tool (ACM Creativity & Cognition 2024).
practical_applications: Same model + similar prompt = similar ideas across users; vary the input, not just ask again.
limitations: Small sample; abstract only.
Reused record from an earlier batch (key kept); not re-read in this session.

title: The Impact of Creativity Training on Creative Performance
authors: Sio, U. N.; Lortie-Forgues, H.
key_findings: 169 studies (844 effect sizes, 48 unpublished); unadjusted 0.53 SD; converging evidence of strong publication bias, adjusted estimates 0.29-0.32 SD; many methodological shortcomings, little improvement over time.
practical_applications: Expect modest gains from any named creativity method; don't promise big effects.
limitations: Abstract/preprint summary only.
Reused record from an earlier batch (key kept); not re-read in this session.

title: Thinking hats and good men: Structured techniques in a problem construction task
authors: Vernon, D.; Hocking, I.
key_findings: Six hats and 'six men' (5W1H) both improved fluency and originality in problem construction vs controls; published abstract and preprint disagree on which technique had the more robust effect.
Authors' 2016 follow-ups: order of hats had no effect (possibly underpowered); a placebo-controlled study found active techniques beat placebo.
practical_applications: Six hats is acceptable as a perspective-switching prompt, but evidence is a handful of small studies; 5W1H questions work about as well.
limitations: Small samples, one lab; search summaries only; no large independent trial found.
Reused record from an earlier batch (key kept); not re-read in this session.

title: Parallel Prototyping Leads to Better Design Results, More Divergence, and Increased Self-Efficacy
authors: Dow, S. P.; Glassco, A.; Kass, J.; Schwarz, M.; Schwartz, D. L.; Klemmer, S. R.
key_findings: Novices designing web ads: parallel prototyping beat serial on all performance measures, produced more diverse prototypes (independent raters), increased self-efficacy, and more positive reactions to critique.
Murphy et al. 2022 reports similar advantages in engineering design.
practical_applications: Make 3 rough directions side by side before polishing one; compare, then iterate the winner.
limitations: Abstract/summaries only; novice sample; one task type.
Reused record from an earlier batch (key kept); not re-read in this session.

title: How Pixar Fosters Collective Creativity
authors: Ed Catmull
key_findings: People learn from postmortems but dislike them, prefer to praise and move on, and 'game the system to avoid confronting the unpleasant'
Techniques: vary the postmortem format (same format finds the same lessons); each group lists top five things to do again and top five not to; use lots of data (rework rates, completeness at handoff)
Dailies: show unfinished work daily so people do not polish the wrong thing in private
practical_applications: Per job: keep-3 / change-3 with data (rerenders, quota used, user verdict)
limitations: Executive's own account; no independent evaluation
Found via search this session (HBR Sept 2008); registry holds a full_text record from an earlier batch; details here from search summaries only.

title: Cognitive architecture and instructional design: 20 years later
authors: John Sweller; Jeroen J. G. van Merrienboer; Fred Paas
key_findings: Reviews 20 years of cognitive load theory: manage load so processing irrelevant to learning is minimised and germane processing optimised within capacity
Grounds the theory in evolutionary psychology and extends it to course-level design and measurement
practical_applications: Cut extraneous load: split-attention, redundancy, transient information
limitations: Full text not reached (login redirect); effects come from instructional settings
Reused record from an earlier batch (key kept); not re-read in this session.

title: Divergent Thinking as an Indicator of Creative Potential
authors: Runco, M. A.; Acar, S.
key_findings: Divergent-thinking (DT) tests estimate creative potential, not achievement; DT is not the same as creative thinking; tests are reliable and moderately predictive, 'far from perfect'.
practical_applications: Many ideas is a means, not the goal: judge final work on originality + fit, not idea count.
limitations: Abstract/excerpts only; later papers flag psychometric problems of DT scores.
Reused record from an earlier batch (key kept); not re-read in this session.

title: The magical number 4 in short-term memory: A reconsideration of mental storage capacity
authors: Nelson Cowan
key_findings: When rehearsal and long-term-memory chunking are prevented, a single central capacity limit averages about 4 chunks (population range about 3 to 5)
Miller's 7 reflects rehearsal and grouping; capacity is counted in chunks, not raw items
Some theories place the limit in duration/decay rather than number (debated in the article)
practical_applications: Max ~4 meaning units per slide/shot
Lists of 3-4 items; group longer lists into categories
Limit new names/numbers per spoken sentence
limitations: Lab tasks with digits/words/shapes, not narratives
Defining a 'chunk' in real sentences is hard
Reused record from an earlier batch (key kept); not re-read in this session.
